words: compelling question; supporting question; enduring issue; credibility; provenance; historiography
cross_subject: ela:W.11-12.7 (short and sustained research projects); ela:W.11-12.8 (gather and assess sources)
notes: The high school research cycle, taught in full on the first US History I research task and used all year: write a compelling question that names an enduring issue (who counts as a citizen, how far federal power reaches), break it into supporting questions, and say where historians agree and disagree about it. Choose sources on purpose: a range of views, kinds of source and makers; judge a source by its maker, date, place, audience and purpose, and by how experts in the field rate it. Grade 11 depth: students build their own question and source set, where earlier grades worked from a question and set the teacher gave.

standard: MA.USI.T1.1; MA.USI.T1.2; MA.USI.T1.3; MA.USI.T1.4; D2.His.4.9-12; D2.His.14.9-12
words: Seven Years' War; Proclamation of 1763; Parliament; representation; boycott; Sons of Liberty; sovereignty
notes: Why the colonies broke with Britain, 1754 to 1775: the French and Indian War inside the global Seven Years' War and its debt; the Proclamation Line, the Stamp, Tea and Intolerable Acts; Patriot answers (boycotts, the Sons of Liberty, the Boston Tea Party) and the Boston and Massachusetts people at the center. Each act is read three ways: as Parliament saw it, as colonists saw it, and as Native nations saw it (Pontiac's War of 1763, led by the Odawa leader Pontiac, came before the Proclamation). The skill: sort economic, intellectual and cultural causes and weigh them, not list them. The Odawa and other Great Lakes nations govern themselves today.

words: natural rights; unalienable; consent of the governed; grievance; equality; rule of law
cross_subject: ela:RI.11-12.9 (founding documents read for their themes and purposes)
notes: The Declaration of Independence read as an argument: its claim (a government that breaks the people's trust may be replaced), its evidence (the list of grievances) and its reasoning from natural rights and consent. Students test the claim of equality against 1776: slavery legal in every colony, women without a vote, and a grievance that calls Native peoples savages. Teacher note: the phrase about Native peoples is discussed as the writers' view, with Native nations' own answer to it; read in full, not hidden. Later readers (Douglass in 1852, Seneca Falls in 1848) turned the same words into claims for their own rights.

words: Continental Army; militia; Loyalist; alliance; encampment; turning point
notes: The war from Lexington and Concord to Yorktown, mapped and dated: Saratoga as the turning point that brought the French alliance; Valley Forge; Washington, Greene and other leaders. The war's many participants: Loyalists; Black soldiers on both sides (the 1st Rhode Island Regiment; Dunmore's 1775 offer of freedom to men who fled to the British); women in the camps; the Haudenosaunee Confederacy split, the Oneida and Tuscarora mostly with the Patriots and most other nations with Britain, and the 1779 Sullivan campaign that burned Haudenosaunee towns. The skill: how a person's significance (Deborah Sampson, James Armistead Lafayette) is judged differently over time. The Haudenosaunee nations govern today.

words: Articles of Confederation; Shays' Rebellion; compromise; ratification; three-fifths clause; federalism
notes: From the Articles (1781) to the Constitution: why a weak central government was chosen, what it could not do, and how Shays' Rebellion in Massachusetts pushed the call for a convention. The Convention's fights and deals: representation (the Great Compromise), slavery (the three-fifths clause, the 1808 slave trade clause, the fugitive slave clause), the executive and ratification. Figures in their time and place (Madison, Hamilton, Franklin, Washington). The skill: judge a decision against its moment and the options on the table, without excusing what it did. Teacher note: the slavery compromises are named plainly as protections of slavery.

words: printing press; pamphlet; partisan press; telegraph; Black press; circulation
notes: News/media literacy, placed in US History I. How news spread from the printing press to the telegraph and, in outline, radio, television and the internet, on a timeline. One case study: newspapers and pamphlets in the Revolution and the ratification debate (the Federalist essays first ran in New York newspapers), or the Black press (Freedom's Journal in 1827, Douglass's North Star in 1847). Each paper is sourced: who owned it, who read it, what it wanted. Hands on the history of the press that US Government builds on when it turns to press freedom.

words: Federalist; Democratic-Republican; political party; judicial review; neutrality; Alien and Sedition Acts
notes: Washington, Adams and Jefferson: Hamilton's financial plan and the first two parties; neutrality and the Jay Treaty; the Alien and Sedition Acts and the Virginia and Kentucky Resolutions; the 1800 election as the first peaceful handover between parties; Marbury v. Madison (1803) and judicial review; the Louisiana Purchase and the embargo. The skill: evaluate each policy's effect on federal power and foreign policy with evidence, and see how party conflict started.

words: spoils system; veto; Indian Removal Act; sovereignty; nullification; Trail of Tears
notes: Andrew Jackson's presidency: the spoils system, the veto of the national bank, the Nullification Crisis with South Carolina, and Indian removal. The Removal Act of 1830; the Cherokee Nation's case in the courts, where the Supreme Court held in Worcester v. Georgia (1832) that Georgia's laws had no force on Cherokee land, and the government removed the nation anyway; the forced marches of the Cherokee, Muscogee (Creek), Choctaw, Chickasaw and Seminole, on which thousands died. Present tense: these nations govern today, many in Oklahoma, and the Supreme Court held in McGirt v. Oklahoma (2020) that the Muscogee (Creek) reservation still exists for federal criminal law. Teacher note: removal named plainly as forced; Cherokee and Muscogee materials from the nations themselves; no simulation of the march.

words: Manifest Destiny; annexation; cession; War of 1812; Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo; territory
notes: Expansion from 1800 to 1854, read from maps: the Louisiana Purchase, the War of 1812, Texas, Oregon, the war with Mexico (1846 to 1848) and the Mexican Cession, and the Gadsden Purchase. Short-term and long-term effects, especially the fight over slavery in new land. Each gain told with the people already there: Native nations (the Comanche, Shoshone and many others, who govern today) and Mexican citizens who became US residents under the 1848 treaty. Grade 11 depth for D2.Geo.2: maps are used as evidence of political and economic dynamics, not only to locate places.

standard: MA.USI.T3.1; MA.USI.T3.2; MA.USI.T3.2a; MA.USI.T3.2c; MA.USI.T3.2d; MA.USI.T3.2e; D2.His.2.9-12; D2.Geo.4.9-12; D2.Geo.10.9-12
words: Transportation Revolution; canal; market economy; textile mill; immigration; famine; labor reform
notes: The North and West, 1800 to 1860: steamboats, the Erie Canal, roads and railroads, and how they tied farms to cities and markets; New England textile mills and machine shops, maritime trade and the new class of merchants and manufacturers; the young women who were most of the mill workforce and their strikes and petitions for a shorter day; Irish famine and German immigration in the 1840s and 1850s. The skill: change and continuity (what changed for a farm family, a mill worker, an immigrant; what stayed), and how a canal or railroad changed land use and trade. Northern mills ran on Southern cotton, taken up in us1-slavery-economy.

words: cotton gin; domestic slave trade; collateral; plantation; enslaved; profit
notes: Why slavery grew after 1800: the cotton gin and cotton's spread west; the domestic slave trade that forced about a million people south and west; Northern mills, banks and insurers that profited (enslaved people used as loan collateral and insured as property). Slavery's place in the industrial North as well as the South. Teacher note: plain facts with the human side, enslaved people's own accounts first; people named as enslaved people, never as slaves alone; no role play or simulation; no business names needed.

words: resistance; rebellion; Underground Railroad; narrative; testimony; limitation
cross_subject: ela:RI.11-12.1 (cite strong evidence from the text)
notes: A primary source research task on one part of enslaved people's lives and resistance: the Stono Rebellion (1739), the Haitian Revolution and its echo in the United States, Nat Turner's rebellion (1831), the Underground Railroad, or daily resistance (work slowdowns, keeping families and faith). The skill: what the sources can and cannot tell, and whose voices they hold or leave out; for example the 1930s interviews of formerly enslaved people, recorded decades later mostly by white interviewers in the segregated South, and trial records written by those who put rebels to death. Teacher note: violence named plainly; no role play.

words: Great Awakening; abolition; suffrage; reform; nativism; Transcendentalism; civil disobedience
notes: Religion and reform, 1730s to 1850s: the Great Awakenings, Republican Motherhood, anti-Catholic nativism. Then a primary source research project on one reform and its ties to others: abolition (Frederick Douglass, Sojourner Truth, and how Northerners and Southerners answered them); women's rights and the 1848 Seneca Falls Convention; Horace Mann and free public schools; schools for deaf and blind students and Dorothea Dix's asylum reform; the Transcendentalists (Emerson, Thoreau, Fuller) and civil disobedience. Students pick one; the class shares findings so each reform is met.

words: sectionalism; Missouri Compromise; popular sovereignty; Fugitive Slave Act; secession; triggering event
notes: How the country came apart, 1820 to 1861: the Midwest's growth and the balance of free and slave states in Congress; the Missouri Compromise, the Compromise of 1850 and its Fugitive Slave Act, the Kansas-Nebraska Act and Bleeding Kansas, the Dred Scott decision (1857, later undone by the 13th and 14th Amendments), Lincoln's election and secession. The skill: tell long-term causes from triggering events and build a historical argument about why war came, with the seceding states' own declarations as evidence that slavery was the central cause.

words: Union; Confederacy; blockade; Emancipation Proclamation; contraband; United States Colored Troops
notes: The war, 1861 to 1865: Lincoln's aims and how his views on slavery and union changed; the blockade; the Emancipation Proclamation and the 180,000 Black men who served in the United States Colored Troops; Davis, Lee and Grant; Antietam, Gettysburg and Vicksburg on the map. Primary sources (diaries, letters, newspapers, photographs, cartoons) on the men and women who fought and served, Harriet Tubman's Combahee River raid and army nurses among them. The skill: how later writers shaped the history, for example the Lost Cause account that recast the war as about states' rights, read against the sources of 1861. Teacher note: battlefield photographs show the dead.

words: Reconstruction; amendment; Freedmen's Bureau; citizenship; equal protection; Black Codes
notes: Reconstruction, 1865 to 1877: Southern destruction; the 13th, 14th and 15th Amendments and the growth of federal power; the Freedmen's Bureau, schools and churches built by freedpeople, and more than 1,500 Black officeholders; Black Codes, Klan terror and the Colfax massacre of 1873; the deal of 1877 that ended federal protection; Northern industry's growth. The skill: critique a secondary work, comparing the early 1900s account that called Reconstruction a failure of Black government with Du Bois's Black Reconstruction (1935) and later historians, by the sources each used. Teacher note: racial terror named plainly.

words: Jim Crow; segregation; separate but equal; disfranchisement; historically Black college; sharecropping
notes: After Reconstruction: one Jim Crow practice studied for its long-term effects on Black education and wealth, such as school segregation or Plessy v. Ferguson (1896), which the Supreme Court overturned for schools in Brown v. Board of Education (1954); and the answers Black Americans built, historically Black colleges and early African American literature (Dunbar, Chesnutt), with Twain's Huckleberry Finn read for how it treats race. Teacher note: lynching named plainly; slurs in period texts are not printed on student pages (rule 6), and the teacher note says how to handle them aloud.

words: Industrial Revolution; entrepreneur; monopoly; trust; labor union; strike; pollution
notes: Industry after 1865: causes (wartime demand, railroads, steel, oil and electricity, inventors and entrepreneurs such as Carnegie and Edison) and consequences joined into one chain: big business and trusts, distrust of monopolies and the Sherman Antitrust Act (1890), growing cities and tenements, pollution and land change around mills and mines, and labor unions and strikes (Haymarket 1886, Homestead 1892, Pullman 1894). The skill: connect consequences to one another, not list them.

words: immigrant; push factor; pull factor; nativism; exclusion; Angel Island; Ellis Island
notes: Why Germans, Irish, Italians, Eastern Europeans, Chinese, Koreans and Japanese came between about 1870 and 1920, and the work they did in industry and on the railroads, from letters, photographs and interviews. Nativism and the Chinese Exclusion Act (1882, in force until 1943); Angel Island and Ellis Island. The skill: how the context of the time shaped how newcomers and the native-born saw one another, and how that context still shapes views today. Teacher note: anti-Chinese violence (Rock Springs, 1885) named plainly; slurs not printed.

words: treaty; reservation; allotment; boarding school; sovereignty; citizenship
notes: The West after 1865, using treaties and laws as sources: the Fort Laramie Treaty of 1868 and the taking of the Black Hills (the Supreme Court held in 1980 that the taking was unlawful; the Lakota nations have refused the payment); wars on the Plains and the Wounded Knee massacre (1890); the Dawes Act (1887) and loss of land; boarding schools, documented in the federal government's own 2022 investigative report. The 14th Amendment's reach: not to Native people (Elk v. Wilkins, 1884; citizenship came in 1924), but to children of Chinese immigrants (Wong Kim Ark, 1898). Present tense: the Lakota and other nations govern today and work to restore language and land. Teacher note: from the nations' own published materials; sacred knowledge left out; no simulation.

words: workforce; suffrage; 19th Amendment; women's club; temperance; ratification
notes: Women's work outside the home after 1865 (factories, offices, teaching, nursing, domestic work) and its effects; one women's political organization researched. Then the long fight for the vote to the 19th Amendment (1920): leaders and groups (Stanton, Anthony, Catt, Paul, Mary Church Terrell, Ida B. Wells), their tactics and their splits, and the resistance, including women who opposed suffrage. The skill: after 1920, who still could not vote (many Black women in the South, Native women before 1924, Asian immigrants barred from citizenship), so the amendment's reach is judged with evidence.

words: Progressivism; muckraker; reform; regulation; child labor; investigative journalism
notes: Progressivism in the early 1900s, from a Progressive's own text or images (Jane Addams, Upton Sinclair, Theodore Roosevelt, Jacob Riis's photographs). One policy researched: the problem it targeted and its short-term and long-term success (the 1916 child labor law, struck down in 1918 and replaced only in 1938; the Pure Food and Drug Act of 1906). News/media literacy NML.T3.2, placed here: how investigative journalists such as Ida Tarbell and Sinclair gathered and checked facts, and how that compares with fact-checking today.

words: civil rights; NAACP; Niagara Movement; accommodation; anti-lynching; Great Migration
notes: How Black Americans pursued civil rights from about 1895 to 1920 and how far they got: Booker T. Washington's and W. E. B. Du Bois's strategies compared from their own words; the Niagara Movement and the NAACP (1909); Ida B. Wells's anti-lynching reporting; the start of the Great Migration. Teacher note: lynching named plainly; images used with care.

standard: MA.USI.T7.5; MA.USI.T7.5a; MA.USI.T7.5b; MA.USI.T7.5c; MA.USI.T7.5d; MA.USI.T7.5e; MA.USI.T7.5f; MA.USI.T7.5g; MA.USI.T7.5h; MA.USI.T7.5i
words: imperialism; annexation; territory; protectorate; Open Door; Roosevelt Corollary
notes: The United States in the world, 1867 to 1914: a research report, with maps and timelines, on one of Alaska (1867), Hawaii (the 1893 overthrow of Queen Liliuokalani and 1898 annexation, which Congress apologized for in 1993), the Spanish-American War and the Philippine-American War, the Open Door, the Roosevelt Corollary, the Platt Amendment and Cuba, the Panama Canal, Dollar Diplomacy or the Mexican Revolution. Present tense: Native Hawaiians and Alaska Native peoples today; Puerto Rico and Guam as US territories now. Teacher note: Philippine-American War deaths named plainly.

words: news; opinion; editorial; op-ed; assertion; verification; inference; sponsor
notes: News/media literacy, placed in US History I beside us1-empire. Tell news from opinion (news article, editorial, editorial cartoon, op-ed); find out who is behind a website (sponsor, author, funding) by reading laterally; check claims and evidence; tell an assertion from a verified fact and evidence from inference. Practised on the 1898 press coverage of the battleship Maine (papers blamed Spain at once; an 1898 navy inquiry said a mine; a 1976 study pointed to a fire inside the ship), then on one current website.

standard: MA.USI.T7.5j; MA.USI.T7.5k; MA.USI.T7.6; MA.USI.T7.7; MA.USI.T7.8; D2.Geo.12.9-12
words: neutrality; submarine warfare; Zimmermann telegram; Fourteen Points; League of Nations; pandemic
notes: World War I: why the United States stayed out and then entered in 1917 (submarine warfare, the Lusitania, the Zimmermann telegram, Wilson's war aims); the American role in the fighting, the Harlem Hellfighters among others; the home front, the Espionage and Sedition Acts and Schenck v. United States (1919); the 1918 to 1920 influenza pandemic and its toll; Wilson's Fourteen Points, the League of Nations, and the Senate's rejection of the treaty, argued in a structured class debate on joining the League. The course ends here; US History II opens in the 1920s.

words: claim; counterclaim; rebuttal; evidence; reasoning; synthesis
cross_subject: ela:W.11-12.1 (argument with claims and counterclaims); ela:W.11-12.9 (draw evidence from texts)
notes: The sourced historical argument, built through US History I: a precise claim, evidence integrated from several sources and interpretations, a counterclaim answered, and the limits of the evidence named; also the sequenced explanation, which says why one event led to another. Students let questions about one source lead to new sources, and spot where sources disagree in order to revise a claim. Grade 11 depth: an essay of several pages on a question of the student's choosing, written at least three times in the year (for example on the causes of the war, Reconstruction and the empire debate).

standard: MA.USII.T1.1; MA.USII.T1.2; MA.USII.T1.3; MA.USII.T1.4; MA.USII.T1.5; MA.USII.T1.8
words: scarcity; supply; demand; profit; financial market; investment; rate of return; GDP
cross_subject: math:F-IF.B.4 (read key features of a graph)
notes: US History II opens with a short economics toolkit used all year: scarcity and trade-offs, goals of economic policy (freedom, efficiency, security, growth, stable prices, full employment), supply and demand with a simple graph, profit as the reward for risk, what moves supply and demand, how financial markets move savings to investment, why an investment's value rises and falls (tracked on paper), and how household, business and government spending set national income. Supply and demand is introduced here and in Economics, since a student may take either first; Economics goes deeper.

words: bank; banking crisis; Federal Reserve; business cycle; fiscal policy; monetary policy; public good
notes: The economy and government across US history: banks and why banking crises happen (the panics of 1907, 1933 and 2008); why the Federal Reserve was created in 1913 and its tools; how wars and technologies drove business cycles (the Civil War, canals and railroads, the space age and the internet); the roles government takes in a market economy (public goods, redistribution, property rights, market failures); taxing, spending and monetary policy at work in the 1930s, the 1970s and 2008. The skill: a cause-effect chain from an event to prices and jobs.

standard: MA.USII.T2.1; MA.USII.T2.1a; MA.USII.T2.1b; MA.USII.T2.1c; MA.USII.T2.1g; MA.USII.T2.1h; MA.USII.T2.1i
words: modernity; traditionalism; Harlem Renaissance; Jazz Age; Prohibition; fundamentalism
notes: Tradition and modernity, about 1913 to 1930, argued from primary sources: the Harlem Renaissance (Langston Hughes, Zora Neale Hurston) and its business and patrons; the Armory Show and modern art; women who served in World War I as nurses and telephone operators; the Scopes trial and the evolution debate; Prohibition and the Jazz Age; the growing visibility of gay and lesbian life in cities. Teacher note: LGBTQ history taught plainly as part of the record (values rule c), at a level that suits grade 12.

words: Red Scare; quota; eugenics; white supremacy; Great Migration; sterilization
notes: The other side of the decade: refugees after World War I, the Red Scare and the 1924 national-origin quotas; the revived Ku Klux Klan, white supremacy, the Tulsa Race Massacre (1921) and the first Great Migration; the eugenics movement, its sterilization laws and Buck v. Bell (1927), which the Court never formally overruled although later cases and the science have rejected its basis; the Lawrence Bread and Roses strike, the Boston police strike and the Sacco and Vanzetti trial. Teacher note: racial terror and forced sterilization named plainly; no slurs printed.

words: Great Depression; stock market crash; unemployment; Dust Bowl; Keynesian; monetarist
notes: The Great Depression worldwide: causes and effects, with two competing explanations compared (a Keynesian account of collapsing spending; a monetarist account of a shrinking money supply). Then a primary source report on how Americans responded: the Bonus Army, farm protests, migrants from the Dust Bowl (the drought and farming practices behind it), the forced removal of Mexican Americans, many of them citizens, and family survival. Grade 12 depth for D2.Geo.9: climate and land use as a cause of migration, with the data.

words: New Deal; relief; recovery; reform; Social Security; labor union; antisemitism
notes: The New Deal through one case study from primary sources (the FDIC, the SEC, the TVA, Social Security, the National Labor Relations Act, the WPA, the Fair Labor Standards Act, the AFL or CIO, the Communist Party, or the America First movement and antisemitism), with the era's people: Hoover, Franklin and Eleanor Roosevelt, Frances Perkins, Huey Long, Charles Coughlin, Charles Lindbergh. Then how well the New Deal worked and for whom (Social Security first left out farm and domestic workers, so many Black workers). The skill: how historians' verdicts relate to the sources they rest on.

words: isolationism; fascism; totalitarian; antisemitism; Lend-Lease; Pearl Harbor
notes: From the Senate's rejection of the League to Pearl Harbor: an argument on how well isolationism served the country (the Neutrality Acts, Lend-Lease); the rise of fascism in Italy and Nazism in Germany, and the racist and antisemitic ideas and laws that led to the Holocaust; why the United States entered the war and declared war on Japan and Germany in December 1941. Teacher note: Nazi propaganda shown only with framing; never role played.

standard: MA.USII.T3.4; MA.USII.T3.5; MA.USII.T3.5a; MA.USII.T3.5b; MA.USII.T3.5c; MA.USII.T3.5d; MA.USII.T3.5e; MA.USII.T3.5f
words: Allies; Axis; appeasement; rearmament; offensive; conference
notes: World War II on the world map: the Allied and Axis powers located; then a primary source study of one road to war (the Rhineland, Munich, the Nazi-Soviet Pact and Poland, Japan's invasion of China and the Nanjing Massacre), one battle and its results (Pearl Harbor, Midway, D-Day, the Bulge, Iwo Jima, Okinawa), or one Allied conference (Yalta, Potsdam). Teacher note: the Nanjing Massacre and battle deaths named plainly; images chosen with care.

words: Holocaust; refugee; quota; liberation; genocide; war crimes trial
notes: How the United States and its allies responded to the Nazi persecution of Jews: refugee quotas and the Evian Conference (1938), the ship St. Louis turned away (1939), what officials knew and when, the War Refugee Board (1944), liberation of the camps by Allied soldiers, and the Nuremberg trials. Teacher note: survivor testimony from recorded collections; no simulation of any kind; graphic images limited and framed.

words: atomic bomb; Manhattan Project; deterrence; arms race; fallout; interpretation
notes: Hiroshima and Nagasaki (August 1945): the reasons given at the time, the human cost (survivors' accounts), and the debate over nuclear weapons from the late 1940s to the early 1960s (the arms race, fallout, civil defense, test bans). The skill: how present-day views shape interpretations of the past, seen in later public fights over how the bombing is remembered and displayed. Teacher note: survivors' accounts chosen for grade 12; more than one defensible answer on the decision.

words: home front; mobilization; incarceration; Executive Order 9066; Double V; Great Migration
notes: Long-term effects of the war at home: growth out of the Depression; the second Great Migration to Northern cities and California; A. Philip Randolph's march threat and the 1941 order against hiring bias in defense work; women in munitions work and noncombat military jobs (pilots, clerks, nurses, the first computer programmers); the forced removal and incarceration of about 120,000 Japanese Americans, two-thirds of them citizens, and of Japanese Canadians; and how two world wars sharpened demands for civil rights. Korematsu (1944) upheld the order; the Supreme Court said in 2018 it was wrong the day it was decided, and Congress apologized and paid redress in 1988. Teacher note: incarceration named plainly, not as relocation.

words: Cold War; containment; communism; Marshall Plan; NATO; flashpoint; space race
notes: The Cold War's causes and containment, from Soviet and American sources: Soviet control of Eastern Europe, the Truman Doctrine, the Marshall Plan, NATO and the Warsaw Pact, the Korean War. Communism as an economic system compared with a market economy; flashpoints from the 1950s to the 1980s located on a world map; Sputnik (1957) and the national push into space and science education.

words: containment; escalation; Gulf of Tonkin; Tet Offensive; antiwar movement; refugee
notes: Vietnam policy under Eisenhower, Kennedy, Johnson and Nixon and its intended and unintended results for Vietnamese and Americans: escalation after the Gulf of Tonkin, Tet (1968), the antiwar movement and veterans' experience, the war in Laos and Cambodia, the fall of Saigon (1975), and Vietnamese, Hmong and Cambodian refugees who came to the United States. Teacher note: the My Lai massacre named plainly; some students' families lived this history.

words: Cuban missile crisis; Great Society; Medicare; War on Poverty; detente; Watergate
notes: Kennedy, Johnson and Nixon from primary sources: the Cuban missile crisis, the Great Society (Medicare, Medicaid, the War on Poverty, the 1965 immigration law), Vietnam policy as each president framed it, Nixon's opening to China and detente, and Watergate. The skill: judge a president's policy from the documents of the time, not only from later memory.

words: GI Bill; suburb; redlining; consumerism; Interstate Highway; Taft-Hartley Act
notes: Postwar America: one domestic policy of Truman or Eisenhower researched (the Fair Deal, the Taft-Hartley Act, the 1956 Federal-Aid Highway Act); the GI Bill, suburbs, television and consumer spending, with who was shut out (redlining maps and restrictive covenants that kept Black families from many suburbs and from GI Bill home loans). Grade 12 depth for D2.Geo.8: how highways and housing policy reshaped city, suburb and countryside, read from maps of one metropolitan area.

words: anti-communism; McCarthyism; loyalty oath; blacklist; Lavender Scare; due process
notes: Domestic communism and anti-communism in the 1950s: real Soviet espionage and the Communist Party in the United States; loyalty programs, the House committee hearings and Hollywood blacklists, and Senator McCarthy's rise and fall; the Lavender Scare, which pushed gay and lesbian federal workers out of their jobs; and the people and institutions who opposed McCarthyism. The skill: tell evidence-based charges from guilt by association. Teacher note: values rule c on the Lavender Scare.

words: civil rights; nonviolence; civil disobedience; integration; boycott; sit-in; Freedom Rides
notes: The African American Civil Rights Movement from primary sources: its roots and goals; Martin Luther King Jr., Rosa Parks, Ella Baker, Fannie Lou Hamer, Malcolm X; the NAACP, SNCC and CORE; Brown v. Board (1954); the Montgomery Bus Boycott, Little Rock and Eisenhower's record; nonviolent civil disobedience and its roots in Gandhi; sit-ins, the Freedom Rides, Birmingham, the March on Washington, Selma; King's assassination (1968). White resistance (Massive Resistance, the murder of Emmett Till). The skill (D2.Civ.12): how people used and challenged laws and courts to change them. Teacher note: violence named plainly; no role play of segregation.

words: Civil Rights Act; Voting Rights Act; fair housing; affirmative action; disparity; demographic
notes: What the 1964 Civil Rights Act and the 1965 Voting Rights Act achieved and how they shaped later rights movements; race relations since then: fair housing (1968), affirmative action and the Supreme Court's 2023 ruling against race-conscious admissions, Shelby County v. Holder (2013) and the Voting Rights Act, gaps in education, health, wealth and incarceration, and the election of Barack Obama (2008). The skill: read demographic data from 1964 to 2010 and map it at more than one scale (county, state, nation) to make a claim about change and continuity. Teacher note: data stated with its source; court rulings stated as the Court decided them.

words: desegregation; busing; METCO; court order; de facto segregation; de jure segregation
notes: School desegregation in the North, through Massachusetts: the METCO program (1966) linking Boston and Springfield students to suburban districts; the 1974 federal court order and the Boston busing crisis; Massachusetts civil rights leaders. Set beside national rulings (Swann, 1971; Milliken v. Bradley, 1974) and, where the teacher can, a case from the student's own region. Teacher note: anti-busing violence named plainly; more than one community's view.

words: social movement; advocacy; Title IX; disability rights; sovereignty; self-determination
notes: One movement studied for its causes, course, tactics and opponents: women's rights (Title IX, the Equal Rights Amendment, Roe v. Wade in 1973 and its overruling in Dobbs in 2022, Sandra Day O'Connor); LGBTQ civil rights (Stonewall, AIDS activism, Goodridge in 2003 and Obergefell in 2015); disability rights (the 1977 sit-ins, the 1975 education law, the ADA and IDEA); the environment (Silent Spring, the clean air and water laws); farmworkers (Cesar Chavez, Dolores Huerta); or Native nations' rights and sovereignty (the Indian Civil Rights Act, Alcatraz, the American Indian Movement, Wounded Knee in 1973, the self-determination laws of the 1970s). Present tense: Native nations govern and revive languages today. Teacher note: values rule c; court rulings stated as decided; students' own views stay theirs.

words: liberalism; conservatism; welfare state; deregulation; union; tax cut
notes: Two traditions read from their own sources: mid-century liberalism (the New Deal legacy, strong unions and manufacturing, welfare programs, regulated industries) and the conservative movement that grew to elect Ronald Reagan (tax cuts, anti-communism, deregulation, the 1981 air traffic controllers' strike). The skill: explain each tradition in terms its supporters would accept, then weigh the evidence of results.

words: Berlin Wall; glasnost; arms control; collapse; satellite state
notes: How the Cold War ended: failing communist economies, reform and protest in Eastern Europe (Solidarity in Poland), US policy and support for resistance to Soviet moves, arms control, the fall of the Berlin Wall (1989) and the Soviet collapse (1991). The skill: weigh internal and external causes rather than credit one leader.

words: computer revolution; genome; immigration law; globalization; diversity
notes: Late 20th and early 21st century trends: the computer and internet revolution, DNA research and the human genome, and Asian and Latin American immigration after the 1965 law ended national-origin quotas. The skill: what changed and what continued, compared with the immigration of 1880 to 1920 studied in grade 11.

words: terrorism; homeland security; surveillance; civil liberties; war powers
notes: How well the federal government answered 21st-century terrorism: the September 11 attacks, the new Department of Homeland Security, the surveillance laws and the debate over them, and the wars in Afghanistan (2001 to 2021) and Iraq (2003 to 2011). The skill: evaluate effectiveness against stated goals with evidence, with more than one defensible answer. Teacher note: some students' families served or were harmed; backlash against Muslim Americans named plainly.

words: audience; presentation; critique; credibility; documentary
cross_subject: ela:W.11-12.7 (sustained research project); ela:SL.11-12.4 (present for an audience)
notes: The grade 12 capstone in US History II: a researched argument on a question from the 1920s to today, adapted for a chosen audience in print, spoken or digital form (a talk, a short documentary, a website), with a structured peer critique of other students' claims, evidence, reasoning and sequence. Grade 12 depth: the student picks the question, builds the source set and answers the strongest counterargument.

standard: MA.GOV.T1.1; MA.GOV.T1.2; MA.GOV.T1.3; MA.GOV.T1.4; D2.Civ.2.9-12; D2.Civ.8.9-12
words: citizenship; politics; republic; oligarchy; autocracy; pluralism; elitism
notes: What government and politics are and why governments exist; citizens, civic groups and government solving a public problem together. Forms of government (direct and representative democracy, republic, monarchy, oligarchy, autocracy) compared across times and places; theories of how American democracy works (republicanism, pluralism, elitism) and the citizen's role in each, with how participation has changed. The skill: test a theory against evidence about who actually takes part.

words: voluntary association; civil society; social capital; nonprofit
notes: Why citizens join voluntary groups: Tocqueville's 1830s account set beside the reform groups met in grade 11 and beside modern writers on civic life and its decline. How government, civil society and markets relate and press on each other. The skill: compare an old and a modern argument with evidence about membership today.

words: popular sovereignty; federalism; social contract; Federalist; Anti-Federalist; ratification
notes: Founding documents read for their central ideas: popular sovereignty, federalism, individual rights, the social contract and natural rights, in the Declaration, the Constitution and a state constitution (Massachusetts's of 1780, the oldest still in force, beside the student's own state's). The Federalist and Anti-Federalist debate (Federalist 10 and 51 against Brutus). A research presentation on how a democratic principle in a founding document changed through later documents (the Reconstruction amendments, the 19th Amendment, the Civil Rights Act), with context and evidence.

words: ideal; liberty; equality; majority rule; minority rights; deliberation
notes: Efforts, past and present, to close the gap between the founding ideals and real political life, from abolition and Reconstruction to today. Then a structured deliberation and a written position on a case where core values pull against each other (liberty and equality, majority rule and minority rights). The skill: deliberate with people who disagree, state the other side fairly, reach a reasoned position. The position is the student's own; the course picks no side.

standard: MA.GOV.T2.1; MA.GOV.T2.2; MA.GOV.T2.3; MA.GOV.T2.4; MA.GOV.T2.5; D2.Civ.1.9-12
words: unitary; confederal; federal; enumerated powers; implied powers; tribal sovereignty; town meeting
notes: How power is divided: unitary, confederal and federal systems; the US Constitution's and a state constitution's grants and limits of power; enumerated and implied powers (McCulloch v. Maryland, 1819); how state and local governments relate in law, money and services, taught for the student's own state, with Massachusetts's open and representative town meetings as one example. Tribal nations as a third sovereign: more than 570 federally recognized nations with their own constitutions, courts and services, and the Supreme Court's line from Worcester (1832) to today.

words: judicial review; independent judiciary; precedent; majority opinion; dissent; appeal
notes: What federal and state courts do, judicial review since Marbury, and why judges are independent. Then core constitutional principles and one Supreme Court case on them, read in its majority and dissent; the student argues for one side and explains what the case shows about how the branches relate. The skill: how the Constitution's powers and limits have changed through interpretation and are still argued.

words: executive order; veto; appointment; cabinet; agency; bureaucracy; regulation
notes: The President's roles and powers, the checks on them, executive orders and judicial appointments. Executive departments and agencies: what they do, with one agency researched for its origins and current work (Defense, the Environmental Protection Agency or the Treasury, or one of the student's own state's executive offices for education, labor or health, as Massachusetts's are in the anchor).

words: checks and balances; separation of powers; court packing; special prosecutor; reconciliation; war powers
notes: How Congress, the President, the courts and the bureaucracy balance each other, judged through historical tests: Franklin Roosevelt's 1937 court plan, the 1973 firing of the Watergate special prosecutor, the use of budget reconciliation for large policy changes, and the fight over who may make war (the War Powers Resolution, 1973). Then an argument on how well the Constitution's design (separation of powers, checks and balances, federalism, rule of law) works today, with recent examples from more than one party.

words: limited government; deregulation; privatization; counterargument; credible evidence
notes: The movement since the 1980s to limit and shrink government: its ideas, leaders and results. Students argue for or against it with credible evidence and answer the strongest counterarguments; both positions are given equal sources. The position is the student's own.

words: civil liberty; civil right; human right; due process; equal protection; incorporation
notes: The documents that protect rights compared: the Bill of Rights, the 14th Amendment and the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948). Then two Supreme Court decisions on individual rights, researched in context and presented to show how rights protection has changed (for example Schenck in 1919 against Brandenburg in 1969 on speech, or Plessy against Brown). The skill: how personal interests and perspectives bear on the reading of rights.

words: free press; First Amendment; prior restraint; censorship; information
notes: News/media literacy, placed in US Government. Why a free flow of information matters in a democracy; press freedom in the First Amendment and in state constitutions (the student's own and Massachusetts's), meaning publishing without government control; how a free press offers competing information about government; and government control of information past and present (the 1798 Sedition Act, World War I, Near v. Minnesota in 1931, the Pentagon Papers case in 1971, censorship in other countries today).

words: political party; platform; primary; campaign finance; turnout; super PAC
notes: How parties grew from the 1790s, how they are organized and what they do, and how candidates and issues are promoted now. Students research party and candidate platforms and read campaign finance, advertising and voter data (turnout by age and group, Citizens United in 2010 as the Court decided it) to draw conclusions about who takes part in elections. Parties are compared on their own published platforms.

words: interest group; lobbying; political action committee; faction; advocacy
notes: Interest groups and political action committees: how they grew from the founding on, their strategies (lobbying, lawsuits, campaigns, protest) and effects, and views on their role from Madison's fear of factions to today. Groups chosen from more than one side of an issue.

standard: MA.GOV.T4.4; MA.GOV.T4.5; MA.NML.T3.1; MA.NML.T3.3; MA.NML.T3.4; MA.NML.T3.5
words: social media; algorithm; news industry; consolidation; misinformation; discerning
notes: News/media literacy NML.T3 placed in US Government beside the government standards on media. What digital news and social media bring to a democracy (speed, volume, many outlets) and what they cost; how new technology widens the reach of media and of business and public interest groups; how ownership consolidation and the move to digital change what news people get; what research shows about media effects on public discussion; and why a careful news consumer strengthens both a life and self-government.

words: public policy; public opinion; intended outcome; unintended consequence; regulation
notes: One past and one current public policy debate compared (labor reform, the environment, disability rights, voting rights or consumer protection), with how parties, interest groups and media shaped opinion each time; the policy judged by its intended and unintended results. Builds directly on the grade 11 Progressive and suffrage studies.

words: policy issue; lobbyist; news report; editorial; advanced search; survey
notes: A current policy issue followed through the news: how parties, interest groups, lobbyists, media and voters push on lawmaking; news reports, social media posts and opinion pieces on it taken apart for evidence, sources and missing views. Students gather information with advanced searches or their own interviews and surveys, then write both a factual report and an editorial on it, with visuals they make, and explain how the two kinds of writing differ (news/media literacy NML.T4.4 and T5.1 to T5.3, placed in US Government).

words: local policy; stakeholder; compromise; position paper; informed action; civic virtue
notes: The course's informed action: in teams, students study a local policy issue they choose, weigh competing views, seek a compromise, judge how well the people and bodies involved have handled it, and find real ways to take part; they produce position papers or a digital product (a multipage site, portfolio or podcast) and may work online with outside experts (news/media literacy NML.T5.4 and T5.5, placed here). Action is the student's choice informed by evidence, never a cause the course picks; adult contact goes through the school.

words: diplomacy; treaty; sanction; foreign aid; covert action; war powers
notes: How nations deal with each other (trade, tourism, diplomacy, treaties, force) and why they come into conflict; the foreign affairs powers of the President and Congress; the tools of US foreign policy, from aid and sanctions to covert action and military intervention; and the forces that shape it (business, labor, interest groups, public opinion, ethnic and religious groups), with grade 11's empire era as the first case.

words: United Nations; NATO; nongovernmental organization; treaty; international law
notes: Governmental and nongovernmental international organizations (NATO, the United Nations, the International Red Cross) and how the United States takes part in them, from the League debate of 1919 to today; how constitutions, laws and treaties keep or strain international order. Then a major world issue researched from varied sources, its likely effect on US policy in one region analyzed, and a position argued that answers opposing views.

words: scarcity; natural resource; human resource; capital; opportunity cost; trade-off; production possibilities curve
cross_subject: math:F-IF.B.4 (read key features of a graph)
notes: Economics opens with scarcity: the resources every good needs (natural, human, capital); choices by consumers and producers with their opportunity costs and trade-offs; broad policy goals (freedom, efficiency, equity, security, growth, stable prices, full employment) and why they conflict. The production possibilities curve is introduced here and used to show choice, opportunity cost, unemployment (a point inside the curve), productivity and growth (the curve moving out).

words: incentive; reward; penalty; interest rate; saver; borrower; voluntary exchange
notes: People respond in predictable ways to rewards and penalties; interest rates as incentives for savers and borrowers; voluntary exchange happens when both sides expect to gain. The skill: trace how an incentive in a policy spreads costs and benefits across different groups.

words: traditional economy; market economy; command economy; mixed economy; property rights; rule of law
notes: How traditional, market, command and mixed economies answer what to produce, how and for whom; how incentives steer production in a market; why clear, enforced property rights and the rule of law matter to a market economy. The United States as a mixed economy, with cases from other countries.

words: demand; supply; equilibrium; price signal; quantity demanded; resource market
notes: Supply and demand in full, with the graph introduced formally here: demand and supply curves, how buyers and sellers together set the equilibrium price and quantity, prices as signals, consumers deciding in the end what gets made, and the same reasoning in product, resource (labor) and financial markets.

words: shift; determinant; elasticity; elastic; inelastic; substitute; complement
notes: What shifts supply and demand (income, tastes, prices of related goods, costs, technology, number of sellers) and how each shift moves equilibrium price and quantity, shown on graphs in product, resource and financial markets. Price elasticity of demand and supply computed from percent changes and used to predict how quantity responds to a price change.

words: price ceiling; price floor; shortage; surplus; rent control; minimum wage; marginal cost
notes: Price and wage controls on the supply and demand graph: a ceiling (rent control) and a floor (minimum wage), with the shortages and surpluses they create and their intended and unintended results. Students build an argument with marginal benefits and marginal costs. Where economists' studies disagree (the size of minimum wage effects on jobs), both lines of evidence are taught; the student's judgment is their own.

words: entrepreneur; profit; sole proprietorship; partnership; corporation; stock; bond; nonprofit
notes: Profit as the reward for the risk of failure; sole proprietorships, partnerships and corporations compared (liability, control, raising money); how firms finance themselves (retained earnings, stock, borrowing) and the trade-offs; the roles of labor unions and nonprofits in a market economy. Builds on the grade 11 rise of the corporation.

standard: MA.ECON.T3.4; MA.ECON.T3.5; MA.ECON.T3.6; MA.ECON.T3.7; D2.Eco.4.9-12; D2.Eco.5.9-12
words: monopoly; oligopoly; perfect competition; market power; marginal revenue; marginal cost
notes: Pure competition, oligopoly and monopoly: their features, how competition among many sellers lowers costs and prices, how firms with market power use marginal analysis to set price and output, and competition on price and on other features. The skill: judge how much competition a real market has and what follows from it, with the grade 11 trusts as a historical case.

words: productivity; human capital; physical capital; technology; wage; standard of living
notes: Why spending on research, equipment, technology and worker training raises productivity, and why higher productivity raises growth and living standards (the production possibilities curve moving out); how a worker's earnings depend on the market value of what they produce and on their productivity.

standard: MA.ECON.T4.1; MA.ECON.T4.3; MA.ECON.T4.4; MA.ECON.T4.6; D2.Eco.6.9-12; D2.Eco.7.9-12
words: public good; market failure; externality; antitrust; natural monopoly; regulation; government failure
notes: Why government acts in markets: public goods and services, market failures and externalities, antitrust laws that promote competition (from the Sherman Act met in grade 11 to today), regulated natural monopolies such as utilities; and how policies can cost more than they return when goals other than efficiency drive them. The skill: weigh a policy's costs and benefits to judge whether it improved a market outcome.

words: revenue; progressive tax; proportional tax; regressive tax; deficit; surplus; national debt; marginal rate
notes: Government budgets: the main revenue and spending categories and their shares at the local, state and federal levels; progressive, proportional and regressive taxes; how changes in spending and taxes move deficits, surpluses and the debt; and (personal finance PFL.T1.3) how federal income tax rates on different incomes have changed since 1950, read from the rate tables. Builds on the 16th Amendment (1913) from grade 11.

words: GDP; economic growth; unemployment rate; inflation; consumer price index; aggregate demand; aggregate supply
notes: How the whole economy is measured: GDP, growth, unemployment and inflation defined and how each is counted (and what each misses), aggregate supply and demand defined; causes of inflation and who gains and loses from it. Students use current indicators to describe the state of the economy and where it may be going.

words: business cycle; expansion; recession; aggregate demand; aggregate supply; money supply
notes: National income, employment and prices as the result of household, business and government spending and production choices; aggregate supply and aggregate demand together setting unemployment and inflation; business cycles shaped by events in US history (the railroad booms and panics of grade 11, wars, new technologies). Students use current data to explain how changes in spending, production and the money supply affect the economy.

words: money; medium of exchange; store of value; unit of account; money supply; Federal Reserve
notes: What money does (medium of exchange, store of value, unit of account); what counts in the money supply; the roles of banks and other financial institutions; how the Federal Reserve System is organized and what it does, set against the fight over a national bank met in grade 11.

words: fiscal policy; monetary policy; interest rate; open market operations; stimulus; stabilization
notes: Fiscal and monetary policy defined; how taxing and spending decisions and the Federal Reserve's tools are used to pursue stable prices, full employment and growth; students evaluate which policy choices suit which conditions (a recession, high inflation), with cases from recent decades.

standard: MA.ECON.T7.1; MA.ECON.T7.2; MA.ECON.T7.3; MA.ECON.T7.4; MA.ECON.T7.8; D2.Eco.14.9-12
words: trade; specialization; absolute advantage; comparative advantage; tariff; quota; free trade
notes: Why individuals, regions and countries trade; absolute and comparative advantage worked from opportunity costs, and why most trade rests on comparative advantage; tariffs and quotas and why countries set them; the arguments for and against free trade weighed with evidence on who gains and who loses.

words: balance of trade; balance of payments; exchange rate; globalization; labor productivity
notes: The balance of trade and the balance of payments; US labor productivity compared with other developed countries; how exchange rate changes affect buying power at home and abroad; how globalization and competition for scarce resources affect growth, labor markets, rights, the environment and income in different nations, and lead to conflict or cooperation.

words: career; wage; salary; benefits; labor market; unemployment
notes: Personal finance: how people choose jobs they qualify for (satisfaction, pay, benefits, growth, location) and how the labor market sets wages; how a recession or a shift in an industry can cut income or end a job. Students sketch a first-year budget for one chosen job.

words: advertising; influencer; payment method; rent-to-own; consumer protection; fee
notes: Personal finance: how advertising and social media move buying, read from studies of their effects; ways to pay (cash, debit and credit cards, checks, rent-to-own) and the true cost of each; the roles of state and federal governments in protecting consumers. Examples are made up, never real brands.

words: principal; interest; compound interest; nominal rate; real rate; retirement account; deposit
notes: Personal finance: banks as businesses that lend depositors' money; principal, simple and compound interest (compound growth worked as growth by a constant percent); real and nominal interest rates; the credit, saving and investing services institutions offer; government policies that encourage saving (retirement and education accounts) and how well they work.

words: regulator; deposit insurance; Federal Reserve; Securities and Exchange Commission; consumer financial protection
notes: Personal finance: how well public agencies protect the banking system, markets and consumers (the Federal Reserve, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, the FDIC, state banking departments, and the SEC's regulation of financial markets), judged with evidence from crises and enforcement records.

words: credit card; annual percentage rate; introductory rate; credit report; credit score; disclosure
notes: Personal finance: a card purchase is a loan, with fees and usually higher rates than other loans; why low introductory rates can jump after a late payment; credit bureaus, reports and scores, how they are used and what leads to denial; the right to full disclosure of loan terms and a free copy of one's own credit report.

words: loan; down payment; term; repossession; garnishment; bankruptcy
cross_subject: math:A-SSE.B.4 (the loan payment formula from a geometric series)
notes: Personal finance: the long-term results of not repaying loans (damaged credit, repossession, wage garnishment, bankruptcy), then a credit plan for a major purchase such as a car or home that compares interest rates and terms and shows the total paid. Numbers are made-up offers, not real lenders.

standard: MA.PFL.T3.7; MA.PFL.T3.8; MA.PFL.T3.9; MA.PFL.T2.6; MA.ECON.T2.11; MA.ECON.T6.6
words: asset; stock; bond; mutual fund; rate of return; diversification; risk
notes: Personal finance and economics: financial markets move money from savers to investors; what a financial asset is and why its value rises and falls; how buyers and sellers set asset prices and so rates of return; why diversifying lowers risk; students track a made-up portfolio of stocks, bonds and funds on paper and write a savings or investment plan for a goal such as college or retirement. No real money and no individual company recommended.

words: insurance; premium; deductible; coverage; identity theft; scam
notes: Personal finance: the purposes of the main kinds of insurance (health, auto, renters or home, life, disability), then cost and coverage compared across several made-up quotes to pick the best fit for a described person; identity theft and how to protect personal information online, by email and by phone.
